docs.text:
College Mentorship Management System (CMMS)

A robust, modern full-stack MERN platform engineering automated faculty–student mentor allocation, concurrency-safe office hour scheduling, immutable meeting audit trails, and role-based departmental analytics.

UCS503P: Software Engineering TIET Patiala MERN Stack Prototype Delivered 14/14 Tests Passed Explore System Design → API Reference GitHub Repository 100% Intra-Dept Allocation 0 Double-Booking Conflicts 14 / 14 Test Cases Passed < 200 ms API Response Latency

docs.title: 📌 Executive Summary
docs.text:
Mentorship programs in higher educational institutions frequently struggle with fragmented communication channels, manual paper/email coordination, mismatched faculty specializations, and unrecorded meetings.

The College Mentorship Management System (CMMS) solves these structural inefficiencies through a unified digital architecture. Built on React 19, Vite, Express 5, Node.js, and MongoDB Atlas, CMMS delivers:

  1. Automated Mentee Allocation: Matches students to faculty advisors based on department affiliation and academic focus areas.
  2. Conflict-Free Office Hour Booking: Faculty publish available time windows; strict server-side concurrency locks block overlapping slots.
  3. Immutable Meeting Audit Trail: Timestamped notes and post-session rating logs provide continuity across semesters.
  4. Role-Based Portals: Dedicated interfaces for Students, Faculty Mentors, and Department Administrators with real-time engagement telemetry.

docs.title: ⚖️ Problem vs. Solution
docs.text: Operational Vector Legacy / Informal Workflow CMMS Digital Platform Mentor Assignment Manual spreadsheet distribution; unbalanced workloads Deterministic intra-department allocation with workload caps Slot Scheduling Ad-hoc emails, corridor walk-ins, frequent overlaps Real-time conflict-free calendar with double-booking prevention Meeting Records Unrecorded or scattered in individual notebooks Centrally indexed, timestamped, immutable session notes Student Feedback Zero quantitative tracking or accountability Post-session 1–5 star ratings and qualitative notes Department Oversight Zero visibility until end-of-semester grievances Live admin dashboard with mentee distribution & activity stats

docs.text:
CMMS operates on a decoupled 3-tier client-server architecture with secure JWT authorization and role-based guards:

        SchedEng["Scheduling & Concurrency Guard"]
        LogEng["Meeting & Notes Logger"]
        MetricEng["Department Analytics Engine"]
    end

    subgraph DataLayer ["Data Layer (MongoDB Atlas + Mongoose)"]
        UDB[("Users & Profiles")]
        MDB[("Mentors & Availability")]
        SDB[("Meetings & Bookings")]
        NDB[("Immutable Notes & Logs")]
        FDB[("Feedback & Ratings")]
    end

    SP --> AuthMid
    FP --> AuthMid
    AP --> AuthMid

    AuthMid --> AllocEng
    AuthMid --> SchedEng
    AuthMid --> LogEng
    AuthMid --> MetricEng

    AllocEng <--> UDB
    AllocEng <--> MDB
    SchedEng <--> SDB

docs.title: ⚡ Core Capabilities
docs.text:
🎯 Intelligent Allocation

Matches incoming students to departmental faculty using academic interest clustering while strictly honoring mentor capacity thresholds.

🔒 Concurrency-Safe Scheduling

Prevents race conditions when multiple students attempt to claim the same office hour slot using atomic status transitions.

📝 Session Archival

Structured post-meeting notes accessible only to involved parties, preserving advising context across academic terms.

📊 Department Telemetry

Department heads monitor faculty workload balance, meeting frequencies, student completion rates, and average satisfaction ratings.

🛡️ Role-Guarded RBAC

Stateless JWT authentication with role claims (Student, Faculty, Admin) and bcrypt password hashing.

🔄 Administrative Override

Allows academic administrators to seamlessly reassign mentees in the event of faculty sabbatical, leave, or workload balancing.

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Week 1 --- Project Pitch Deck
docs.text: The project direction and initial requirements were being established by the team, while I was getting familiar with the overall CMMS workflow and the modules we would need to design and implement.

docs.title: Week 2 --- Project Proposal
docs.text: I followed the project proposal and system requirements to understand the expected roles, workflows, and backend requirements, particularly the data that would eventually need to be stored and managed using MongoDB.

docs.title: Week 3 --- System Design and Module Planning
docs.text: I reviewed the system design being developed by the team, with particular attention to the use-case diagram and data-flow diagrams because these would later determine the structure of the backend and database.

docs.title: Week 4 --- Diagram Corrections and Backend Preparation
docs.text:
Worked on correcting anomalies and inconsistencies in the system design diagrams, specifically the UML use-case diagram and the Level 0/Level 1 data-flow diagrams. Reviewed the diagrams against the project requirements and checked that actors, use cases, processes, data stores, and data flows represented the same system behavior across the different diagrams. Corrected mismatched or unclear relationships and flows so that the final diagrams were internally consistent and could be used as the basis for implementation.

Also took responsibility for the backend portion of the project, which will be implemented using MongoDB for data storage. Mapped the backend responsibility to the system's main data entities, including users, assignments, meetings, and meeting notes, based on the data stores already represented in the DFDs. Backend coding has not been started yet; the current work has focused on making the diagrams accurate and preparing the database/backend structure that will be implemented in the next stage. The diagram corrections were important because the final implementation needs to follow the finalized system design rather than building the backend around inconsistent or outdated flows.

docs.title: Week 5 --- Backend Implementation and API Development
docs.text:
Started the implementation of the backend for the Mentorship Management System based on the finalized system design and data-flow diagrams. Set up the Node.js and Express.js backend structure and configured MongoDB Atlas for persistent data storage using Mongoose. Created the required database models for users, students, faculty/mentors, assignments, meetings, feedback, and meeting notes according to the main entities identified during the system design phase.

Implemented REST APIs for managing users, mentors, students, assignments, meetings, feedback, and notes. Added functionality for user registration and login, mentor allocation, meeting booking, meeting history, mentor availability, assignment management, meeting notes, and department-level summary information. Tested the APIs using Postman and verified that the data was being correctly stored, retrieved, updated, and related through MongoDB.

Implemented authentication using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and added role-based authorization for students, faculty, and department administrators. This ensures that operations such as mentor requests, mentor approval, and student reassignment can be restricted according to the responsibilities of each user role.

Also implemented and tested the mentor allocation workflow, where a student can submit a mentor request and a faculty member can review and approve the request. The approval process updates the assignment and associates the student with the selected mentor. Additional testing was carried out for administrator functions such as reassigning mentees and viewing department summary statistics.

Integrated the backend APIs with the frontend application and tested the major role-based workflows through the application interface. Verified the student, faculty, and administrator dashboards and checked that actions performed through the frontend were reflected correctly in the backend and database. The main backend functionality is now operational and provides the foundation for further testing, refinement, and deployment of the complete system.

docs.title: Aaditya Bansal
docs.text:
Week 1  Project Pitch Deck

Built the initial CMMS pitch deck (.pptx + .pdf), covering the problem statement, motivation, and proposed solution.

Structured the deck as a 4-slide minimalist pitch: Introduction, Motivation, Problem Statement, Solution. Wrote the core framing: mentorship currently runs on informal email/office hours coordination, with three specific failure points no shared calendar (missed meetings), no tracking (departments can't see meeting frequency or outcomes), and no workload visibility (mentee counts skew unevenly across faculty with no way to see it). Defined the four solution pillars: Automated Allocation, Seamless Scheduling, Progress Dashboards, Continuous Monitoring. These later became the system's four actual backend modules almost unchanged, so the early framing held up well. Used a dark-charcoal-on-off-white palette with a geometric monogram mark instead of stock or AI-generated imagery, specifically to avoid the deck reading as templated.

                                            Week 2 Project Proposal

Wrote the full project proposal (.tex + .pdf), following the course's proposal structure guide section by section.

Structured it into: Introduction/Problem Statement, Objectives, Methodology, Feasibility, Timeline, Resources and Budget. Objectives: one primary goal plus five specific, action-oriented sub-goals (matching, scheduling, dashboards, meeting notes, admin visibility), matching the SMART framing from the guide. Methodology: architecture and tech stack (MERN React frontend, Node/Express API, MongoDB), module breakdown (Allocation, Scheduling, Meeting Notes, Dashboards), execution/integration approach (weekly iterations, manual deploy), and testing/validation criteria (assignment correctness, meeting completion rate, admin visibility, user satisfaction survey). Made an explicit scope-reduction decision to fit the 12-week timeline: dropped automated workload-balancing in allocation (replaced with manual admin reassignment, since admins can already see mentee counts), dropped structured milestones (replaced with a single free-text meeting note field), and dropped CI/CD plus automated testing for this stage. Documented all three as intentional, reversible scope cuts rather than gaps. Added a Feasibility section (Technical / Operational / Economic), each point tied to something already stated elsewhere in the proposal rather than generic boilerplate. Proofread the whole document to strip informal punctuation (em-dashes used as parentheticals) that reads as AI-generated, replacing each with a colon, comma, or a split sentence depending on what actually fit the meaning.

                          Week 3 and   Week 4  — Use-Case Diagram, DFDs, and Allocation Module

Split my time between finishing the system design diagrams and starting backend work on the allocation module.

Use-case diagram

Modeled 3 actors (Student, Faculty, Department Admin) against 11 use cases inside a CMMS system boundary, following standard UML use-case notation rather than an informal box and line sketch. Added a shared Register / Login use case and connected all three actors to it, since every role needs auth. Used a proper relation from Book Meeting Slot to Check Booking Conflict, to show that conflict checking is a mandatory sub-step of booking, not an optional one — deliberately did not use anywhere it wasn't semantically correct (caught and removed one incorrect relation between two different actors' use cases during review). Cross-checked the use-case diagram against the DFDs afterward and found one inconsistency: the use-case diagram listed "Monitor Faculty Workload" as a distinct admin action, but the DFD only showed one generic "metrics" data flow to Admin. Fixed by splitting the DFD's admin-facing flow into separate Mentorship Metrics and Workload Stats flows so both diagrams agree.

DFDs

Level 0 (context diagram): CMMS as a single process, 3 external entities, labeled bidirectional data flows. Level 1: decomposed process 0 into the four real modules (1.0 Allocation, 2.0 Scheduling, 3.0 Meeting Notes, 4.0 Reporting/Dashboard) with four data stores (Users, Assignments, Meetings, Notes). Kept Assignments as its own data store (D2) separate from Users (D1) deliberately — mentor-student pairing is relationship data, not identity data, and conflating the two would mean every reassignment writes to the same table as login credentials. Used the standard "duplicate entity" convention (Student/Faculty/Admin*, marked with the corner-cut notation) on the output side of Level 1, so the return flow arrows from the Reporting process don't have to snake back across the entire diagram to reach the original entity boxes.

                                           Week 5 — Auth, Seeding & Allocation Engine

Finished login API with JWT + bcrypt (10-round hashing), role encoded in the token so route guards don't need extra DB calls. Added ProtectedRoute.jsx so unauthorized users get redirected before the page loads. Seeded 25+ mock records (CSE faculty + advisees) for testing. Built the allocation engine — matches students to mentors by department. Tested 100% correct, no cross-department mismatches. Built the "My Mentor" view for students. Closed M2 (Allocation Engine) on time.

                                          Week 6 — Scheduling Engine Start + Gantt Chart & Prototype Report

Started Phase 3: booking system. Built API for faculty to publish office-hour slots. Started calendar UI — fetching/showing open slots first, booking logic next. Split scheduling into 4 steps (create slots → fetch available → check conflict → log booking). Harshveer started on the double-booking conflict query in parallel. Put together the 12-week Gantt chart covering all 6 phases and milestones (M1–M6). Drafted the first version of the Prototype Stage Report (architecture, DFDs, ER diagram, DB schema, API routes) — to be finalized once dashboards and testing wrap up.

docs.title: Week 1 - Project Understanding and Initial Planning
docs.text:
I started by understanding the purpose and scope of the CMMS project and the problems it aims to solve in the faculty-student mentorship process. I reviewed the initial discussions with the team and studied how the existing informal mentorship process could be converted into a structured digital workflow.

I contributed to the early planning by discussing the main users of the system, their expected interactions, and the major functions that would be required. I also helped organize the initial ideas so that the problem statement and proposed solution could be represented clearly in the project documentation.

docs.title: Week 2 - Requirement Analysis and Proposal Development
docs.text:
During this week, I worked alongside the team on reviewing the project requirements and understanding how they would translate into actual system functionality. I focused on the different responsibilities of students, faculty members, and department administrators and how their activities would connect within the platform.

I contributed to reviewing the project proposal and checking whether the proposed objectives and features were consistent with the problem identified earlier. I also participated in discussions about the system modules and helped relate the functional requirements to the later design and implementation stages.

This helped establish a clearer structure for the project before moving further into system modelling.

docs.title: Week 3 - System Modelling and Diagram Development
docs.text:
I took a more active role in the system-design phase this week. I worked with the team on developing and reviewing the UML use-case diagram and the data-flow diagrams for the proposed CMMS system.

I helped map the interactions between the three main actors, Student, Faculty, and Department Admin, and the functions they would perform within the system. I also worked on representing the major processes and information flows in the Level 0 and Level 1 DFDs.

A major part of my contribution was checking whether the diagrams accurately reflected the requirements discussed earlier. I compared the relationships between actors, processes, data stores, and flows and discussed changes with the team wherever something appeared unclear or inconsistent.

I also helped connect the system design with the planned modules such as allocation, scheduling, meeting notes, and reporting/dashboard functionality. This gave me a better understanding of how the diagrams would eventually guide the backend and database implementation.

docs.title: Week 4 - Diagram Validation, Database Planning and Implementation Preparation
docs.text:
This week, I continued working on the system design and took greater responsibility for validating the diagrams before implementation. I reviewed the UML use-case diagram and Level 0/Level 1 DFDs together rather than treating them as separate documents.

I checked that the actors and their actions in the use-case diagram were represented correctly in the DFDs, and that the processes, data stores, and data flows followed the same overall workflow. I participated in identifying ambiguous relationships and unnecessary or mismatched flows and helped discuss the corrections with the team.

I also contributed to the planning of the backend data structure by studying the information that would need to be maintained by the system. This included understanding entities such as users, assignments, meetings, and meeting notes and considering how these would relate to the processes shown in the DFDs.

Another part of my work was maintaining consistency between the project requirements, diagrams, and documentation. Whenever a design decision was changed, I helped check its effect on the other project materials so that different parts of the project did not describe conflicting behaviour.

I also coordinated with the team regarding the transition from system design to implementation. My focus was on making sure that the finalized diagrams provided a clear reference for the development work and that the team had a common understanding of the workflow before backend development progressed further.

By the end of this stage, my role had expanded from primarily understanding the project and assisting with documentation to actively contributing to system modelling, diagram validation, database planning, and coordination between the design and implementation phases.

docs.title: Week 5 - Frontend Implementation
docs.text:
This week I moved from the system-design and planning work into active frontend development, translating the use-case diagram and requirement discussions from earlier weeks into the actual React application structure.

I started by setting up the React single-page application and organizing the project into a component structure that reflected the three user roles identified in the use-case diagram, Student, Faculty, and Department Admin. I worked on scaffolding separate route groups and layout components for each role so that the dashboards could be developed independently while sharing common UI elements like navigation, headers, and reusable form components.

I contributed to building the core UI screens discussed during the requirement-analysis stage, including the student view for browsing and requesting mentors, the faculty view for managing office-hour slots and mentee rosters, and the initial admin view for monitoring department-level activity. I focused on keeping the component hierarchy consistent with the processes mapped out in the Level 0 and Level 1 DFDs, so that each screen aligned clearly with a specific system function rather than mixing unrelated actions together.

I also worked on the design system groundwork, establishing consistent styling, spacing, and reusable components (buttons, cards, form inputs, modals) so that the three dashboards would feel part of one unified platform rather than three disconnected interfaces. Alongside this, I paid attention to basic accessibility considerations, such as proper labeling on form fields and sufficient contrast in the UI, since this had been noted as a requirement earlier in the project.

Since the backend APIs were still being finalized in parallel, I worked with mock data and placeholder API calls structured to match the data entities discussed during database planning, users, assignments, meetings, and meeting notes, so that the frontend components would need minimal rework once they were connected to the real endpoints.

I coordinated with the team to make sure the screens under development matched the actor interactions defined in the use-case diagram, and flagged a few places where the original diagram didn't fully account for edge cases in the UI (such as what a student sees before being assigned a mentor). We discussed and resolved these gaps together, and I updated the relevant component logic accordingly.

By the end of this week, the foundational frontend structure was in place across all three role-based views, giving the team a working visual reference for the platform and a clear base to connect to the backend APIs in the coming weeks.

docs.title: ⚙️ Core Modules & Engineering Algorithms
docs.text: The College Mentorship Management System (CMMS) is engineered around four core backend services designed to automate operational processes and prevent runtime data conflicts.

docs.title: 1. 🎯 Automated Allocation Engine
docs.text: The Allocation Engine matches incoming students to faculty mentors within their department while strictly balancing workload distributions.

docs.title: Algorithmic Strategy
docs.text:
1. Department Isolation: Students and mentors are partitioned strictly by academic department: $\(\text{Dept}(\text{Student}) \equiv \text{Dept}(\text{Mentor})\)$
  2. Focus Area Affinity: Mentors whose researchAreas overlap with the student's stated focusArea are prioritized.
  3. Capacity Constraint: A mentor is eligible for assignment only if their active mentee count does not exceed capacity: $\(\text{CurrentCount}(\text{Mentor}) < \text{MaxCapacity}(\text{Mentor})\)$
  4. Workload Balancing: Among eligible mentors with matching affinity, the student is assigned to the mentor with the minimum current load.
flowchart TD
    Start([Start Student Allocation]) --> FilterDept[Filter Faculty by Department]
    FilterDept --> CheckCap{Faculty has capacity?}
    CheckCap -- No --> Reject[Flag Unallocated for Admin Review]
    CheckCap -- Yes --> CheckAffinity[Rank by Focus Area Match]
    CheckAffinity --> MinLoad[Select Faculty with Min Active Mentees]
    MinLoad --> Assign[Create Assignment Record]
    Assign --> IncCount[Increment Faculty Mentee Count]
    IncCount --> End([Allocation Confirmed])

docs.title: 2. 🔒 Concurrency-Safe Scheduling Engine
docs.text: One of the most critical challenges in appointment scheduling is race condition vulnerability: two students attempting to book the exact same open consultation slot at the same millisecond.

docs.title: Mechanism & Concurrency Guard
docs.text:
CMMS implements a 2-stage concurrency barrier:

  1. Database-Level Unique Constraint: A compound unique index on { mentor: 1, slotDateTime: 1 } prevents overlapping bookings at the storage layer.
  2. Atomic Query & Mutate: Booking requests execute via atomic conditional updates:
// Atomically reserve slot if status is still AVAILABLE
const reservedSlot = await Meeting.findOneAndUpdate(
  {
    _id: slotId,
    mentor: mentorId,
    status: 'AVAILABLE' // Concurrency predicate
  },
  {
    $set: {
      student: req.user.studentId,
      status: 'SCHEDULED',
      agenda: req.body.agenda,
      bookedAt: new Date()
    }
  },
  { new: true }
);

if (!reservedSlot) {
  // Slot was claimed by a concurrent transaction
  return res.status(409).json({
    success: false,
    message: 'Conflict: Slot has already been reserved by another student.'
  });
}

This guarantees zero double-bookings without requiring heavy distributed locks or blocking threads.

docs.title: 3. 📝 Immutable Meeting Logging & Audit Trail
docs.text:
Mentorship programs require an accountable historical record across semesters. CMMS implements append-only meeting records:

  • Sealed Records: Once a meeting concludes, the faculty mentor logs notes and action items.
  • Immutability Principle: Note records have immutable: true configured on timestamps and cannot be deleted or modified by students.
  • Action Item Tracking: Action items are indexed as arrays of strings, enabling mentees to track deliverable progress prior to subsequent appointments.

docs.title: 4. 📊 Department Analytics Engine
docs.text:
The Department Analytics Engine powers the Administrative Dashboard by computing real-time metrics across all collections:

  • Mentee Coverage: Ratio of total students allocated vs. awaiting mentor assignment.
  • Engagement Velocity: Total completed consultation sessions over weekly and monthly intervals.
  • Workload Variance: Standard deviation of mentee counts across faculty members, highlighting over-burdened or under-utilized advisors.
  • Quality Index: Rolling average of student feedback scores (1–5) grouped by department and academic year.

docs.title: 📋 System Requirements Specification (SRS)
docs.text: This document formalizes the engineering requirements for the College Mentorship Management System (CMMS) as specified for the UCS503P capstone evaluation.

docs.title: FR-1: Authentication & Identity Management
docs.text:
• FR-1.1: The system shall permit new users to register with an institutional email (@thapar.edu), full name, role (STUDENT, FACULTY, ADMIN), and academic department.
  • FR-1.2: Passwords shall be cryptographically hashed using bcrypt with a minimum work factor of 10 rounds prior to database insertion.
  • FR-1.3: Upon successful credential validation, the system shall issue a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) containing user ID, role, and department claims with an expiration window of 24 hours.
  • FR-1.4: The system shall prevent duplicate registrations using the same email address, returning an explicit HTTP 400 Bad Request.

docs.title: FR-2: Mentor Allocation Engine
docs.text:
• FR-2.1: The system shall execute automated intra-department mentor allocation, matching students exclusively with faculty mentors belonging to the same academic department.
  • FR-2.2: The allocation algorithm shall balance advisee counts across faculty, capping allocations at each mentor's predefined maxCapacity.
  • FR-2.3: Department Administrators shall possess capabilities to execute batch allocations or perform individual manual mentee reassignments.

docs.title: FR-3: Office Hour Scheduling & Concurrency Control
docs.text:
• FR-3.1: Faculty mentors shall define and publish consultation time windows (date, start time, end time, venue/virtual link).
  • FR-3.2: Students shall view unreserved consultation slots published by their assigned mentor and book an appointment with a stated agenda.
  • FR-3.3: The scheduling engine shall guarantee conflict-free booking through atomic status locking, rejecting concurrent attempts to claim the same time slot with HTTP 409 Conflict.
  • FR-3.4: Both student and mentor shall have capabilities to cancel an appointment up to 2 hours prior to scheduled start time, resetting slot availability.

docs.title: FR-4: Post-Meeting Logging & Action Items
docs.text:
• FR-4.1: Immediately following an appointment, the faculty mentor shall record comprehensive summary notes, discussion points, and action items.
  • FR-4.2: Meeting notes shall be immutable once submitted, maintaining an audit trail with UTC timestamping.
  • FR-4.3: Both mentor and the respective mentee shall retain permanent read access to chronological meeting history.

docs.title: FR-5: Session Feedback & Ratings
docs.text:
• FR-5.1: Upon completion of a meeting, the student shall be prompted to submit a quantitative rating (1 to 5 stars) and optional qualitative feedback.
  • FR-5.2: The system shall restrict feedback submissions to one verified entry per completed meeting.

docs.title: FR-6: Departmental Analytics & Dashboards
docs.text:
• FR-6.1: The system shall provide distinct dashboard interfaces tailored to Student, Faculty Mentor, and Department Administrator personas.
  • FR-6.2: The Admin portal shall compute and display live aggregate statistics: total active pairings, meetings conducted this term, faculty workload distribution, and department satisfaction averages.

docs.title: NFR-1: Performance & Response Latency
docs.text:
• The system shall respond to 95% of API requests within 200 milliseconds under standard campus network conditions.
  • Database read queries (such as roster queries and slot lookups) shall utilize indexed fields (mentor_id, student_id, slotDateTime) to avoid collection scans.

docs.title: NFR-2: Concurrency & Transaction Safety
docs.text: • The system shall handle concurrent booking requests gracefully without data corruption, guaranteeing zero double-bookings under concurrent client load.

docs.title: NFR-3: Security & Data Privacy
docs.text:
• All external communication shall be enforced over TLS/HTTPS.
  • Sensitive student academic logs and session notes shall only be accessible to the involved student, assigned mentor, and authorized department heads.
  • Route-level security middleware shall block cross-role privilege escalation attempts with HTTP 403 Forbidden.

docs.title: NFR-4: Availability & Reliability
docs.text: • The backend services and database cluster shall maintain target operational uptime of 99.5% during the academic semester.

docs.title: NFR-5: Maintainability & Modularity
docs.text:
• Clean separation of concerns across Model-Route-Controller layers on the backend, and component-service patterns on the frontend.
  • RESTful conventions adhered to for all resource URI paths and HTTP method verbs.

docs.title: 🏗️ System Architecture & High-Level Design
docs.text:
The College Mentorship Management System (CMMS) is architected as a modular, 3-tier client-server application adhering to modern web engineering principles. By strictly decoupling presentation logic, API orchestration, and persistence, CMMS ensures high scalability, low coupling, and rigorous security boundaries.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Client Layer (React 19 + Vite)              │
│       Student Portal  │  Faculty Portal  │ Admin Dashboard  │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │ HTTPS / JSON (RESTful)
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Application Layer (Node.js + Express 5)     │
│   Auth & RBAC Middleware  │  Routing  │  Controllers        │
│   Allocation Service      │  Scheduling & Concurrency Guard │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                               │ Mongoose ODM / Driver
                               ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 Data Layer (MongoDB Atlas Cluster)          │
│   Users · Mentors · Students · Meetings · Notes · Feedback  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: 1. Presentation Layer (Frontend)
docs.text:
• Framework: React 19 bootstrapped with Vite for sub-second hot-module reloading and optimized production bundles.
  • Routing: React Router v7 providing protected route guards based on authenticated user roles (STUDENT, FACULTY, ADMIN).
  • State Management: Centralized AuthContext maintaining JWT tokens, user profiles, and session states without external heavy boilerplate.
  • Styling: Component-scoped CSS modules ensuring an accessible, responsive dashboard layout optimized across desktop, tablet, and mobile screens.

docs.title: 2. Application Layer (Backend REST API)
docs.text:
• Runtime: Node.js LTS with Express 5 framework.
  • Authentication: Stateless JSON Web Tokens (JWT) signed with HMAC-SHA256 containing user ID and authorization roles.
  • Security Middleware:
  • authMiddleware.js: Validates bearer token signatures and decodes identity claims.
  • roleMiddleware.js: Restricts endpoint access to specific roles (e.g., preventing students from triggering mentor allocation or viewing admin analytics).
  • Concurrency Guard: Atomic database queries with optimistic concurrency control to prevent double-booking of meeting slots during high concurrent traffic.

docs.title: 3. Data Persistence Layer (Database)
docs.text:
• Database: MongoDB Atlas cloud cluster.
  • Data Modeling: Mongoose 8 Object Data Modeling (ODM) providing strict schema validation, referential integrity via ObjectId relations, and compound indexes for fast lookups.

docs.title: 🔒 Security Architecture
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Client as User (Browser)
    participant Auth as Express Auth Middleware
    participant Controller as Resource Controller
    participant DB as MongoDB Atlas

    Client->>Auth: HTTP Request with Bearer JWT
    alt Token Missing or Expired
        Auth-->>Client: 401 Unauthorized
    else Invalid Signature
        Auth-->>Client: 401 Invalid Token
    else Valid Token
        Auth->>Auth: Check Role Claim against Route Guard
        alt Role Unauthorized
            Auth-->>Client: 403 Forbidden
        else Role Authorized
            Auth->>Controller: Forward sanitized request (req.user)
            Controller->>DB: Execute Query / Mutation
            DB-->>Controller: Return Database Document
            Controller-->>Client: 200 OK + JSON Payload
        end
    end

docs.title: Stage 1: Student & Faculty Registration
docs.text:
1. Student registers with institutional email (@thapar.edu) and selects department & specialization.
  2. Faculty registers with credentials, research domains, office location, and maximum mentee load.
  3. System issues encrypted JWT tokens and initializes profile records.

docs.title: Stage 2: Automated Allocation
docs.text:
1. Department Admin triggers allocation run or manual reassignment.
  2. System executes intra-department matching: $\(\text{Department}(\text{Student}) = \text{Department}(\text{Mentor}) \quad \wedge \quad \text{CurrentMentees} < \text{Capacity}\)$
  3. Student and Faculty receive pairing notifications on their respective portals.

docs.title: Stage 3: Availability & Conflict-Free Booking
docs.text:
1. Faculty designates recurring or one-off consultation windows.
  2. Student selects an available slot and submits an appointment agenda.
  3. Concurrency guard validates slot availability in an atomic transaction; status transitions to SCHEDULED.

docs.title: Stage 4: Meeting Execution & Audit Logging
docs.text:
1. Meeting takes place (in-person or virtual).
  2. Faculty accesses meeting dashboard and inputs official summary notes, milestones achieved, and follow-up deadlines.
  3. Student accesses feedback portal and submits structured feedback (1–5 rating + optional comments).
  4. All records are permanently sealed with UTC timestamps in MongoDB.

Decomposes the concurrency-protected booking engine:

        P2_4 -->|Meeting Alert Notification| Faculty
    else Slot Already Claimed
        P2_3 -->>|HTTP 409 Conflict Rejection| Student
    end

docs.title: 🗄️ Persistent Data Store Directory
docs.text: Store ID Name Underlying Collection Scope & Purpose D1 User & Profile DB users, students, mentors Authentication credentials, department affiliations, research focus tags. D2 Allocation DB assignments Active and historical student-mentor mappings with start/end timestamps. D3 Scheduling DB meetings Available slots, booked sessions, recurrence schedules, cancellation states. D4 Meeting Notes & Logs DB notes, feedbacks Immutable post-meeting discussions, follow-up goals, and student satisfaction ratings.

docs.title: 🗃️ Entity Relationship (ER) Diagram & Schemas
docs.text: The persistence tier of CMMS is implemented using MongoDB Atlas with Mongoose ODM. While MongoDB is a document-oriented database, CMMS maintains strict normalized relational integrity through Mongoose ObjectId references, schema-level validation constraints, and foreign key relationships.

docs.title: 1. User Schema
docs.text:
Core identity record supporting authentication and authorization across all system personas. 

const userSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  name: { type: String, required: true, trim: true },
  email: { type: String, required: true, unique: true, lowercase: true },
  password: { type: String, required: true }, // bcrypt 10-round hash
  role: { 
    type: String, 
    required: true, 
    enum: ['STUDENT', 'FACULTY', 'ADMIN'],
    default: 'STUDENT'
  },
  department: { type: String, required: true },
  createdAt: { type: Date, default: Date.now }
});

docs.title: 2. Student Schema
docs.text:
Specific student demographic and advisory status profile. 

const studentSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  user: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'User', required: true },
  rollNumber: { type: String, required: true, unique: true },
  academicYear: { type: Number, required: true, min: 1, max: 5 },
  focusArea: { type: String, required: true },
  assignedMentor: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Mentor' },
  status: { type: String, enum: ['ACTIVE', 'GRADUATED'], default: 'ACTIVE' }
});

docs.title: 3. Mentor Schema
docs.text:
Faculty advisory profile with capacity management and office availability. 

const mentorSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  user: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'User', required: true },
  designation: { type: String, required: true },
  researchAreas: [{ type: String }],
  maxCapacity: { type: Number, default: 15 },
  currentMenteeCount: { type: Number, default: 0 },
  officeLocation: { type: String, required: true },
  availability: { type: String, default: 'Mon-Fri 10:00-12:00' }
});

docs.title: 4. Meeting Schema
docs.text:
Represents an appointment slot or confirmed session. 

const meetingSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  mentor: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Mentor', required: true },
  student: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Student', required: true },
  slotDateTime: { type: Date, required: true },
  durationMinutes: { type: Number, default: 30 },
  status: { 
    type: String, 
    enum: ['SCHEDULED', 'COMPLETED', 'CANCELLED'],
    default: 'SCHEDULED' 
  },
  agenda: { type: String, required: true },
  mode: { type: String, enum: ['IN_PERSON', 'ONLINE'], default: 'IN_PERSON' }
});

// Compound unique index to enforce conflict-free booking per mentor
meetingSchema.index({ mentor: 1, slotDateTime: 1 }, { unique: true });

docs.title: 5. Note Schema
docs.text:
Immutable audit log of meeting proceedings. 

const noteSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  meeting: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Meeting', required: true },
  mentor: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Mentor', required: true },
  student: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Student', required: true },
  content: { type: String, required: true },
  actionItems: [{ type: String }],
  createdAt: { type: Date, default: Date.now, immutable: true }
});

docs.title: 6. Feedback Schema
docs.text:
Student evaluation and satisfaction rating. 

const feedbackSchema = new mongoose.Schema({
  meeting: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Meeting', required: true, unique: true },
  student: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Student', required: true },
  mentor: { type: mongoose.Schema.Types.ObjectId, ref: 'Mentor', required: true },
  rating: { type: Number, required: true, min: 1, max: 5 },
  comments: { type: String, trim: true },
  createdAt: { type: Date, default: Date.now }
});

docs.title: 1. Student (ROLE_STUDENT)
docs.text: The mentee pursuing undergraduate or postgraduate studies within the department. - Academic Profile: Configures degree department and primary interest areas (e.g., AI/ML, Cloud Computing, Cyber Security, Systems). - Advisory Relationship: Views designated faculty mentor with contact information and research profile. - Appointment Scheduling: Browses real-time calendar availability published by their assigned mentor and reserves slots. - History & Reflection: Accesses archived notes from past discussions and submits post-session ratings and reflections.

docs.title: 2. Faculty Mentor (ROLE_FACULTY)
docs.text: The academic advisor responsible for guiding students through educational and career milestones. - Slot Management: Creates, modifies, and publishes weekly office hour windows (start time, end time, location/mode). - Roster Management: Inspects all active mentees, academic standings, and previous meeting frequencies. - Meeting Administration: Accepts or reschedules appointment requests; records immutable summary notes and assigned action items immediately following each session.

docs.title: 3. Department Administrator (ROLE_ADMIN)
docs.text: Head of Department (HoD) or designated academic coordinator overseeing mentorship health. - Allocation Governance: Triggers batch mentorship assignment algorithms; balances mentor-to-mentee ratios across senior and junior faculty. - Exception Handling: Manually overrides or reassigns students when faculty members go on sabbatical or study leave. - Executive Analytics: Monitors department-wide engagement metrics, active vs. inactive pairings, and aggregate satisfaction scores.

docs.title: ⚡ Concurrency Stress Test Analysis (TC-09)
docs.text:
To validate double-booking prevention, an automated load script dispatched 50 simultaneous HTTP requests targeting the same mentor and slot timestamp (2026-09-22T10:00:00.000Z):

Dispatched: 50 concurrent booking threads
├─ Thread #01 (HTTP 201 Created) -> Successfully locked slot
├─ Thread #02 (HTTP 409 Conflict) -> Rejected by atomic lock
├─ Thread #03 (HTTP 409 Conflict) -> Rejected by atomic lock
...
└─ Thread #50 (HTTP 409 Conflict) -> Rejected by atomic lock

Summary:
- Total Successful Bookings: 1
- Total Rejected Collisions: 49
- Double-Booking Rate: 0.00%

The combination of MongoDB unique compound indexing and Mongoose atomic conditional find-and-modify ensures strict linearizability for appointment reservations.
